newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Mobutu, Kabila stay silent on Zaire peace ideas.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu, Kabila stay silent on Zaire peace ideas.

text.p: Zaire's ailing president and the rebels seeking to end his 32-year reign stayed silent on Tuesday about new ideas for a ceasefire and negotiations.
As American, French and Belgian troops massed on Zaire's border, poised to evacuate Westerners if chaos breaks out, politicians in Kinshasa squabbled over the vacant premiership.
International pressure for an end to fighting in the east of the vast country built up but both President Mobutu Sese Seko and rebel leader Laurent Kabila hid their cards.
The rebels have seized about a quarter of Africa's third largest country since their campaign began last October.
They are still about 1,000 km (600 miles) east of Kinshasa but they have mineral-rich Shaba province in their sights and so far Zaire's ragged army has failed to put up a fight.
South African sources said Kabila had dropped a demand for direct talks with Mobutu and agreed to negotiate with a team appointed by the 66-year-old president.
But the government sources, close to South African mediation in the Zaire crisis, told Reuters Kabila was only prepared to negotiate once and the outcome had to be conclusive.
Neither the rebels nor Mobutu's camp commented on the report.
South African emissaries who met Mobutu in Kinshasa on Sunday said he would reply to the new peace ideas within 48 hours.
The deadline was Tuesday night and Zaire's state television said on Tuesday the president's spokesman, Kabuya Lumuna, would make a statement on Mobutu's behalf in the evening.
Mobutu and Kabila have sent teams to Lome, Togo, for a special Organisation of African Unity (OAU) summit on the Zaire crisis starting on Wednesday.
Senior American and French officials, seeking to overcome arguments in Africa and forge a common policy to prevent Zaire breaking up, were in Lome for the talks.
The new Franco-American joint effort on Zaire was evident in Brazzaville on Tuesday where about 1,000 troops from the two allies and Belgium were camped at the airport.
The force was being readied to cross the Zaire river to neighbouring Kinshasa and evacuate thousands of Westerners from Zaire if the crisis degenerated.
Kinshasa was calm on Tuesday but the sprawling city of about three million people was intently following confusing political developments.

The failure to win the war or arrange a peace cost Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo his job. He resigned on Monday but he and his government remain in office until a successor is found -- a potentially lengthy process despite the critical hour.

Opposition parties in the transitional parliament must pick a candidate, for Mobutu's approval, but at a meeting on Tuesday some argued that Kabila join negotiations before a new government is formed.
"We must incorporate the rebels in all consultations. There is no point in forming a government that may only last a matter of days," said Engineer Dyongo, an opposition member.
"Mobutu is trying to save his own skin. We cannot have a government in Kinshasa when we don't know how much territory Kinshasa will control tomorrow," he added.

A host of aspirants for the premiership have thrown their hats into the ring despite the daunting nature of the job. But for ordinary Kinshasa residents, the favourite is without doubt longtime Mobutu foe Etienne Tshisekedi.
It is unclear whether a Tshisekedi government would cooperate with Mobutu or attempt to strike a separate deal with the rebels.
A Zambian Foreign Ministry official said on Tuesday Zambia had evacuated the families of its diplomatic staff in Kinshasa and the southeast mining centre of Lubumbashi because of the war.
In Cape Town, Sadako Ogata, head of the U.N. refugee agency, criticised the international community over Zaire and called for an African rapid intervention force to intervene in conflicts.
Some 400,000 Rwandan and Burundian refugees are unaccounted for in Zaire since fleeing when civil war began last October.
Kabila supporters seized Zaire's embassy in the Ugandan capital Kampala on Monday, set ablaze a Zairean flag and broke a portrait of Mobutu before being expelled by police, diplomats said.
Kinshasa accuses Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi of sending in troops to fight alongside rebels. All three deny the charges.
